p.src: Now, after Aunt Xue had heard the letter from Xue Ke, she called the young servant in and asked, “Did you hear your master say exactly how he came to kill the man?” The servant replied, “I did not hear it very clearly either. That day Master Xue told Second Master about it.” As he spoke, he looked back, and only after seeing that no one was there did he continue, “Master said that ever since the terrible turmoil at home, he had lost all heart for anything, and so he meant to go south to purchase goods. That day he thought of asking someone to travel with him; the man lived more than two hundred li south of our city. Master went to look for him and happened to meet Jiang Yuhan, who had once been his intimate friend, entering the city with several young actors. Master ate and drank with him in a tavern, but the wine waiter kept casting sidelong glances at Jiang Yuhan, which angered Master. Later Jiang Yuhan left. The next day Master invited the man he had gone to find to drink with him. After drinking, he recalled the previous day’s affair and ordered the waiter to change the wine. When the waiter was slow in coming, Master began to curse him. The fellow would not submit, so Master picked up a wine bowl and struck at him. Who would have thought the fellow was a ruffian too? He thrust his head forward and dared Master to hit him. Master smashed the bowl once against his skull. Blood gushed out, and he fell to the ground. At first he was still cursing, but afterward he said nothing more.” Aunt Xue asked, “Was there no one there to restrain them?” The servant replied, “I did not hear Master say anything about that, so I would not dare speak recklessly.” Aunt Xue said, “Go and rest for now.” The servant assented and went out. Aunt Xue then went in person to see Lady Wang and asked her to intercede with Jia Zheng. After asking about the whole affair, Jia Zheng could only give a noncommittal answer. He merely said they should wait until Xue Ke submitted his petition and see what ruling the local magistrate made before deciding what to do.

p.src: The silver brought here has been spent on payments to everyone high and low in the yamen. Elder Brother is not suffering too severely in prison, so please set your mind at ease, Madam. The only trouble is that the people here are very devious: neither the dead man’s relatives nor the witnesses will yield, and even the friend whom Elder Brother invited is siding with them. Li Xiang and I are both strangers here, but fortunately we found a capable adviser. Only after promising him silver did we obtain a plan: we must draw in Wu Liang, who was drinking with Elder Brother, have someone stand surety to get him released, promise him silver, and make him settle the dispute. If he refuses, we are to say that he killed Zhang San and is openly shifting the blame onto a stranger. He will not be able to withstand that pressure, and then the matter will be easy to handle. I followed his advice, and Wu Liang was indeed released. We are now buying over the dead man’s relatives and the witnesses, and we have drawn up another petition. It was submitted the day before yesterday, and the ruling arrived today. You will understand when you read the copy of the petition.

p.src: The petitioner, So-and-so, submits this plea to redress the injustice suffered by his elder brother through an unforeseen calamity. Your humble student’s own elder brother, Xue Pan, is a native of Nanjing and presently resides in the Western Capital. On a certain day of a certain month and year, he took capital with him and set out southward to trade. Only a few days after his departure, a household servant brought word home that he had become involved in a homicide. Your humble student immediately hastened to Your Excellency’s jurisdiction and learned that his brother had accidentally injured a man surnamed Zhang and had been cast into prison. According to his brother’s tearful account, he had never known the man surnamed Zhang and bore him no grudge whatever. A quarrel happened to arise over changing the wine. Your humble student’s brother dashed the wine onto the ground just as Zhang San bent down to pick something up; his hand slipped, and the wine bowl accidentally struck Zhang San on the crown of the head, causing his death. By Your Excellency’s grace he was detained and interrogated; fearing torture, my brother confessed to having caused death in a fight. We look up to Your Excellency’s heavenlike benevolence: discerning that an injustice may have occurred, you have not yet rendered final judgment. As my brother is in custody, his submission of a petition in his own defense would contravene the regulations. Mindful of the bond between brothers, your humble student risks death to submit this plea on his behalf. Prostrate, I beg Your Excellency in your mercy to grant it, summon the witnesses, and examine them face to face. No grace could be greater. Your humble student and his entire household shall look up to your boundless benevolence with gratitude forever without end. In deepest urgency, this petition is respectfully submitted.

p.src: The examination at the place where the corpse lay produced conclusive evidence. Moreover, no torture was employed; your brother himself confessed to killing the man in a fight, and his deposition is on record. You have now come from afar and did not witness the event. How dare you fabricate a story and lodge a false accusation? By rights you should be punished, but in consideration of your earnest concern for your brother, you are pardoned for the present. Petition denied.

p.src: When Aunt Xue heard this, she dismissed the page and immediately went once more to the Jia residence, where she explained the circumstances to Lady Wang and implored Jia Zheng to help. Jia Zheng would agree only to ask someone to plead with the magistrate; he refused to hear of offering money or gifts. Fearing that this would be of no use, Aunt Xue begged Xifeng to speak to Jia Lian; only after several thousand taels had been spent was the magistrate bought over. Xue Ke likewise succeeded in arranging matters at his end. The magistrate then hung out the court tablet and took his seat, summoning all the neighborhood guarantors, witnesses, relatives of the deceased, and others concerned, while Xue Pan was brought out of prison. The clerks of the criminal office called every name in turn. The magistrate ordered the local constable to confirm his original deposition, then called upon the deceased's mother, Widow Zhang Wang, and his uncle Zhang Er for questioning. Weeping, Widow Zhang Wang testified, “My husband was Zhang Da. We lived in the southern countryside, and he died eighteen years ago. My eldest and second sons died too. All I had left was this son who has now been killed, Zhang San. He was twenty-three this year and had not yet taken a wife. Our family was poor and could not support him, so he worked as a stable hand at the Li family inn. At noon that day, someone from the Li family inn came for me and said, ‘Your son has been beaten to death.’ My just and merciful lord, I nearly died of fright. I ran there and saw my son lying on the ground, his head split and bleeding, still gasping for breath. He could not answer when I spoke to him, and before long he died. I wanted to seize this little bastard and fight him to the death.” The runners gave a warning shout. Widow Zhang Wang kowtowed and said, “I beg Your Honor to redress my wrong. He was the only son I had left.” The magistrate ordered her to withdraw, then questioned a man from the Li family inn: “Was Zhang San a hired hand at your establishment?” Li Er replied, “He was not a regular hired hand; he tended the horses and fodder.” The magistrate said, “At the examination of the corpse that day, you said Zhang San had been killed when Xue Pan struck him with a bowl. p.src: Master Xue lost his temper and flung the wine toward Zhang San's face; somehow the bowl struck him on the head. I saw this with my own eyes.” “Nonsense!” said the magistrate. At the examination of the corpse, Xue Pan himself admitted that he had killed the man by striking him with the bowl, and you said you witnessed it. Why does your testimony differ today? Slap his mouth!” The runners acknowledged the order and were about to beat him when Wu Liang pleaded, “Xue Pan truly did not fight with Zhang San. The wine bowl struck his head by accident. If Your Honor will question Xue Pan, it will be a great mercy.” The magistrate ordered Xue Pan brought forward and asked, “What grudge did you really bear Zhang San? Tell the truth about precisely how he died.” Xue Pan said, “I beg Your Excellency for mercy. I truly did not strike him. Because he refused to change the wine, I meant to splash him with it, but my hand slipped and the bowl accidentally struck his head. I hurried to staunch the blood, but nothing would stop it. He lost so much blood that after a little while he died. At the examination the other day, I feared Your Excellency would have me beaten, so I said I had struck him with the bowl. I beg only that Your Honor show mercy.” The magistrate thundered, “You muddleheaded wretch! When I asked how you had struck him, you confessed that you did so because you were angry when he refused to change the wine; today you claim the bowl struck him by accident.” The magistrate made a great show of threatening the rod and the press, but Xue Pan steadfastly adhered to his story. The magistrate ordered the coroner to report truthfully the injuries recorded at the earlier examination of the corpse. The coroner reported, “When Zhang San's body was examined the other day, no injuries were found apart from a wound from a piece of porcelain at the crown of the skull, one inch and seven-tenths long and five-tenths deep. The skin was split, and the crown bone was cracked and broken to a depth of three-tenths. It was indeed an injury caused by an accidental collision.” The magistrate checked that this agreed with the postmortem report. Though he knew full well that the clerks had altered the injuries to make them appear lighter, he raised no objection and carelessly ordered the depositions signed. Widow Zhang Wang cried out, “My just and merciful lord! The other day I heard that there were many other injuries. How have they all disappeared today?” The magistrate said, “This woman talks nonsense. The postmortem report is here before us. Do you know nothing of it?” He summoned Zhang Er, the deceased's uncle, and asked, “Your nephew is dead. How many injuries do you know him to have had?” Zhang Er hastily testified, “One injury on his head.” “There, you see,” said the magistrate. He ordered a clerk to show the postmortem report to Widow Zhang Wang and had the local constable and the deceased's uncle point out its details to her. The witnesses who had personally signed at the examination had all testified that there had been no fight and that the death had not resulted from a brawl. He therefore ordered them to sign depositions declaring it a case of accidental injury. Xue Pan was remanded to prison pending ratification of the verdict; the others were released into the custody of their original guarantors, and the court adjourned. Widow Zhang Wang wept and shrieked in protest, until the magistrate ordered the runners to drive her out. Zhang Er also admonished her, saying, “It truly was an accident. How can you falsely accuse someone? His Excellency has now judged the matter clearly, so make no more trouble.”

p.src: Outside the court, Xue Ke learned exactly what had happened. Delighted, he sent someone home with the news. Once the ratified judgment returned, they could arrange payment to redeem the offense, so for the moment he stayed and waited for news. He heard people along the road saying in twos and threes that an imperial consort had died and that the Emperor had suspended court for three days. As the place was not far from the imperial tombs, the magistrate would be occupied with official duties and preparing the road, and was unlikely to have any leisure for some time. There was no benefit in remaining, so Xue Ke decided instead to visit his brother in prison and reassure him: “I am going home and will return in a few days.” Xue Pan, fearing that his mother would suffer from anxiety, sent word saying, “I am all right. After we spend money at the yamen a few more times, I shall be able to come home. Only do not begrudge the money.”

p.src: Xue Ke left Li Xiang there to attend to matters and went straight home. On seeing Aunt Xue, he related how the magistrate had shown partiality and how he had judged the case, ultimately ruling it accidental injury. If they later spent a little more silver on the dead man's family, the offence could certainly be redeemed and the affair would be over. Aunt Xue was somewhat relieved when she heard this and said, “I have been longing for you to come home and look after things. I really ought to go and pay my respects at the Jia household; besides, now that Imperial Consort Zhou has passed away, they go into the Palace every day, leaving the house quite deserted. I have been thinking of going over to help your aunt and keep her company, but then there would be no one left in our own house. Your arrival could not have come at a better time.” Xue Ke said, “While I was away, I heard that the Jia family's imperial consort had died, and that was why I hurried back. Our Consort Yuan was perfectly well—how could anyone say she was dead?” Aunt Xue replied, “She did fall ill once last year, but she recovered. This time we had heard nothing of Consort Yuan suffering from any illness. We had only heard that the Old Lady in that house had been rather unwell a few days earlier and would see Her Highness Consort Yuan whenever she closed her eyes. Everyone was anxious, but when they made inquiries, they found that nothing was amiss. Then, the night before last, the Old Lady said with her own lips, ‘Why has Consort Yuan come here all by herself?’ Everyone took it merely for something her illness had made her imagine and refused to believe it. The Old Lady went on, ‘You do not believe me, but Consort Yuan also told me that glory and prosperity soon come to an end, and that one must withdraw while there is still time.’ They all said, ‘Who has never had such thoughts? Such reflections on the past and future naturally occupy the mind of someone advanced in years.’ So they paid no particular heed to it. But early the very next morning, an uproar arose in the Palace: Her Highness was gravely ill, and all titled ladies were summoned to enter and inquire after her health. They were overcome with alarm and suspicion and hurried into the Palace. Before they had even returned, word had already reached our house that Imperial Consort Zhou had passed away. Just think: the false rumour outside and the suspicions within the family happened to coincide. Is that not extraordinary?” Baochai said, “Not only were the rumours outside confused and mistaken; even at home, the moment everyone heard the words ‘Her Highness,’ they were thrown into a bustle, and only afterward did they understand. Over the last two days, some of the maids and old serving-women from that household have come and said that they knew all along it was not our own imperial consort. I asked, ‘How could you be so sure?’ They replied, ‘Several years ago, in the first month, someone from another province recommended a fortune-teller who was said to be remarkably accurate. The Old Lady had Consort Yuan's Eight Characters mixed in among those of the maids and sent them out for him to calculate. Of them all, he singled out the young lady born on the first day of the first month, saying that her hour of birth must have been recorded incorrectly; otherwise, she was truly a person of exalted destiny and could not possibly remain in that household. The Master and the others told him that, whether the hour was right or wrong, he should proceed with the calculation according to the Eight Characters.

This time we had heard nothing of Consort Yuan suffering from any illness.
We had only heard that the Old Lady in that house had been rather unwell a few days earlier and would see Her Highness Consort Yuan whenever she closed her eyes.
Everyone was anxious, but when they made inquiries, they found that nothing was amiss.
Then, the night before last, the Old Lady said with her own lips, ‘Why has Consort Yuan come here all by herself?’
Everyone took it merely for something her illness had made her imagine and refused to believe it.
The Old Lady went on, ‘You do not believe me, but Consort Yuan also told me that glory and prosperity soon come to an end, and that one must withdraw while there is still time.’
They all said, ‘Who has never had such thoughts?
Such reflections on the past and future naturally occupy the mind of someone advanced in years.’
So they paid no particular heed to it.
But early the very next morning, an uproar arose in the Palace: Her Highness was gravely ill, and all titled ladies were summoned to enter and inquire after her health.
They were overcome with alarm and suspicion and hurried into the Palace.
Before they had even returned, word had already reached our house that Imperial Consort Zhou had passed away.
Just think: the false rumour outside and the suspicions within the family happened to coincide. Is that not extraordinary?”

Baochai said, “Not only were the rumours outside confused and mistaken; even at home, the moment everyone heard the words ‘Her Highness,’ they were thrown into a bustle, and only afterward did they understand.
Over the last two days, some of the maids and old serving-women from that household have come and said that they knew all along it was not our own imperial consort.
I asked, ‘How could you be so sure?’
They replied, ‘Several years ago, in the first month, someone from another province recommended a fortune-teller who was said to be remarkably accurate.
The Old Lady had Consort Yuan's Eight Characters mixed in among those of the maids and sent them out for him to calculate.

u.src: Of them all, he singled out the young lady born on the first day of the first month, saying that her hour of birth must have been recorded incorrectly; otherwise, she was truly a person of exalted destiny and could not possibly remain in that household.
The Master and the others told him that, whether the hour was right or wrong, he should proceed with the calculation according to the Eight Characters.

p.src: The fortune-teller then said that within the four characters bing-yin of the first month in the jia-shen year were the signs of the Injured Officer and ruined wealth; only the shen character contained the Proper Officer, emolument, and travelling horse. This meant that the family could not keep her at home, though thus far there seemed nothing especially auspicious. The day was yi-mao, and in early spring the wood element flourishes. Although this indicated the Peer, who could have known that the more it was matched, the better it would become? It was like fine timber, which must be hewn and carved ever more before it can become a great vessel. What particularly pleased him was that some xin metal in the hour pillar was noble, and that the Proper Officer, emolument, and travelling horse concealed in si alone were flourishing. This, he said, was the ‘Flying Heavenly Emolument Horse’ configuration. He also spoke of something called ‘the day's emolument returning to the hour,’ which was exceedingly noble, and said that the Heavenly and Monthly Virtues occupied her natal destiny, so that in her exalted station she would receive the favour of the imperial chambers. If this young lady's hour of birth was correct, she was certain to become an imperial mistress and consort. Did that not prove his calculation correct? We also remember him saying that, regrettably, her glory and prosperity would not last long; he feared that when a yin year and a mao month arrived, one Peer would follow another and one Robber of Wealth another. It would be like fine wood carved in pursuit of exquisite delicacy until its very substance was no longer sound. They had forgotten all those words and merely rushed about in blind confusion. Only then did I remember and tell our young mistress that this year is certainly not a yin year and a mao month.’” Before Baochai had finished, Xue Ke broke in urgently, “Never mind other people's affairs for now. Since there is such a divinely gifted fortune-teller, I wonder what baleful star rules my elder brother's fate this year, that he should meet with such an unforeseen calamity. Quickly write out his Eight Characters so that I can take them to be calculated and learn whether he faces any further danger.” Baochai replied, “He came from another province. I do not know whether he is still in the capital now.”

p.src: With that settled, they made arrangements for Aunt Xue to visit the Jia residence. When she arrived, only Li Wan, Tanchun, and the others were at home to receive her. They immediately asked, “How is Cousin Xue’s case?” Aunt Xue replied, “Nothing will be decided until the case is referred to the higher authorities, but it seems unlikely now that he will receive the death penalty.” Only then did everyone feel relieved. Tanchun then said, “Last night Mother was thinking aloud that when our household was in trouble before, we relied entirely upon your help, Aunt; but now that your own family is in difficulty, she scarcely knows how to broach the matter. She simply cannot set her mind at ease.” “I too have been distressed at home,” said Aunt Xue. But your elder cousin had met with disaster, your second cousin had gone away to attend to the case, and with only your sister left at home, what could she possibly manage? Besides, our daughter-in-law is not one who understands how matters should be handled, so I could not get away to come here. At present the magistrate there is also overwhelmed with preparations for duties connected with Imperial Consort Zhou and cannot conclude the case. Only after your second cousin returned was I able to come and see you.” Li Wan said, “It would be even better if you would stay here for a few days, Aunt.” Aunt Xue nodded. “I should like to stay here and keep you girls company. It is only that your Cousin Baochai will be rather lonely.” Xichun said, “If you are worried about her, Aunt, why not invite Cousin Baochai to come too?” Aunt Xue replied with a smile, “That would never do.” “Why not?” asked Xichun. “She used to live here before, did she not?” “You do not understand,” said Li Wan. “Her family is in trouble now. How could she come?” Xichun took this explanation at face value and did not like to ask any more. While they were still talking, Grandmother Jia and the others returned. On seeing Aunt Xue, they did not even pause to exchange greetings before asking about Xue Pan’s case. Aunt Xue related the whole story in detail. Baoyu, listening nearby, heard the part concerning Jiang Yuhan. He did not ask about it before everyone, but wondered to himself, “Since he has returned to the capital, why has he not come to see me?” He also noticed that Baochai had not come and could not imagine the reason. As he sat there lost in thought, Daiyu happened to arrive to pay her respects. Baoyu’s spirits lifted a little. His thoughts of Baochai were interrupted, and he ate supper at the Old Lady’s with the other girls. When everyone dispersed, Aunt Xue made do with a room in the Old Lady’s adjoining suite.

p.src: Baoyu returned to his own room and changed his clothes. Suddenly remembering the sash Jiang Yuhan had given him, he asked Xiren, “Do you still have that red sash you did not wear that year?” “I have put it away,” said Xiren. “Why do you ask about it?” “No reason. I was only asking,” said Baoyu. Xiren said, “Did you not just hear that Master Xue’s association with such scoundrels ended in a matter of life and death? Why bring up those people again? Instead of troubling yourself over such things for nothing, you would do better to sit quietly with your books and put all these trifles out of your mind.” Baoyu said, “I am not getting into any mischief. I merely happened to remember it. It makes no difference whether you have it or not; I only asked one question, and you all have so much to say.” Xiren smiled. “It is not that I mean to nag. Once a person has learned to read and understand proper principles, he should strive to better himself. Then even when the person dearest to him comes, she will be pleased by what she sees and respect him for it.” Prompted by Xiren’s remark, Baoyu exclaimed, “Good heavens! Just now at the Old Lady’s there were so many people that I did not speak to Cousin Daiyu. She paid no attention to me either, and when we dispersed, she left first. She must be in her room now. I shall be back presently.” With that, he started out. “Do come back quickly,” called Xiren. “It was I who raised the subject, and now I have gone and stirred up your enthusiasm.”

p.src: Baoyu made no reply. With his head lowered, he went straight to the Naiad’s House. There he found Daiyu leaning over a table, reading. He went up to her and said with a smile, “So you came back early, Cousin.” Daiyu smiled too. “You paid no attention to me. What was there for me to stay for?” “There were so many people talking that I could not get a word in,” Baoyu explained with a smile, “and that was why I did not speak to you.” As he spoke, he looked at the book Daiyu was reading. He could not recognize a single character in it. Some looked like the character “芍,” others like “茫”; one resembled “大” with a hooked “九” beside it and a “五” added in the middle; another had “五” and “六” above with a “木” added, and yet another “五” below. The stranger they looked, the more perplexed he became. “You have advanced further than ever of late, Cousin,” he said. “Now you are reading the script of heaven itself.” Daiyu gave a little laugh. “A fine scholar you are, never even to have seen qin tablature!” “Of course I know what qin tablature is,” said Baoyu, “but why can I not recognize a single character in it? Can you read them?” “If I could not, why would I be looking at it?” Daiyu replied. “I do not believe you,” said Baoyu. “I have never heard that you could play the qin. Several qins hang in our study. The year before last, a gentleman who frequented our house—Ji Haogu, or some such name—came to visit, and Father asked him to play a piece. He took them down but said none was fit to play, adding, ‘If you are interested, sir, I shall bring my own qin another day and seek your instruction.’ I suppose Father did not understand the instrument either, for the man never came back. How is it that you have been hiding such an accomplishment?” Daiyu replied, “I can hardly claim that I truly know how to play. The other day, when I was feeling a little better, I was browsing through the large bookcase and found a set of qin manuals. They were most refined and fascinating. Their explanations of the instrument’s principles were very sound, and their descriptions of technique were clear. Playing truly was a means by which the ancients stilled the mind and cultivated their nature. In Yangzhou I heard the art discussed with some care and even learned a little myself; but after I stopped practicing, what skill I had simply vanished. It is indeed true that ‘after three days without playing, thorns grow upon the hands.’ The pieces I looked at the other day contained no accompanying texts, only the names of the compositions. So I found another volume elsewhere that included the texts of the pieces, and only then did the study become interesting. Still, it is truly difficult to learn how to play well. The books say that when Shi Kuang played the qin, he could summon wind and thunder, dragons and phoenixes; that even the Sage Confucius studied the qin under Shi Xiang and, upon hearing a single composition, knew it portrayed King Wen; and that the melodies ‘High Mountains’ and ‘Flowing Water’ were fortunate enough to find a kindred listener.” At these words, her eyelids fluttered faintly, and she slowly lowered her head.

p.src: Baoyu was listening with delight and said, “Dear cousin, what you have just told me is truly fascinating. But I did not recognize any of the characters I saw above. Won’t you teach me a few?” Daiyu replied, “There is no need to teach you. Once they are explained, you will understand them at once.” Baoyu said, “I am a muddle-headed fellow. You must teach me the one with the character ‘大’ and a hook added to it, with the character ‘五’ in the middle.” Daiyu laughed. “The characters ‘大’ and ‘九’ mean that the left thumb is to press the ninth stud of the qin, while the hook together with ‘五’ means that the right hand is to hook the fifth string. They do not form a single character, but indicate a single note, and it is extremely easy. There are also techniques called yin, rou, chuo, zhu, zhuang, zou, fei, and tui, all of which concern the movements of the hands.” Baoyu was so delighted that he waved his arms and stamped his feet. “Dear cousin, since you understand the principles of the qin, why don’t we begin learning it?” Daiyu said, “The qin signifies restraint. The ancients devised it for the cultivation of the self and the nurturing of one’s nature, to curb licentiousness and banish extravagance. If one wishes to play the qin, one must choose a quiet chamber or lofty studio, or else the upper floor of a tall building, a place among woods and rocks, a mountaintop, or the water’s edge. Then one must wait for a time when heaven and earth are clear and harmonious, when the breeze is pure and the moon bright; burn incense and sit in stillness, allowing no outward thoughts to disturb the mind and keeping the vital energies in harmony. Only then can one’s spirit commune with the numinous and attain the subtlety of the Way. That is why the ancients said, ‘A true appreciator of music is hard to find.’ If no true appreciator is at hand, one would do better to play alone before the pure breeze and bright moon, the green pines and fantastic rocks, the wild apes and aged cranes, thereby giving expression to one’s feelings. Only then will one prove worthy of the qin. There is another requirement: one’s fingering must be good, and the tones one draws forth must be fine. If one is determined to play, one must first arrange one’s cap and robes neatly, wearing either a crane-feather cloak or a deep robe, so that one resembles the figures of antiquity and is worthy of this instrument of the sages. Then, after washing one’s hands and burning incense, one seats oneself beside the couch, places the qin on the table, and sits opposite its fifth stud, aligned with the center of one’s body. Only then may both hands be raised at ease, with mind and body alike held upright. One must also understand lightness and weight, speed and slowness, and be able to contract or extend one’s movements with perfect ease, while maintaining a grave and dignified bearing.” Baoyu said, “We only want to learn it for amusement. If it requires so much ceremony, it will be difficult indeed.”

p.src: As the two were speaking, Zijuan came in. Seeing Baoyu, she smiled and said, “Second Master Bao, you seem very cheerful today.” Baoyu laughed. “What cousin has been explaining has opened my eyes completely, so the more I hear, the more I want to hear.” Zijuan said, “That is not what I meant by your being cheerful. I meant your coming over to our side.” Baoyu said, “Cousin was unwell before, and I was afraid that making a commotion would vex her. Besides, I have been attending school, so it must have seemed as though I had grown distant.” Before he had finished, Zijuan said, “Our young lady has only just recovered. Since you put it that way, Second Master, you have sat here long enough and should let her rest. You must not keep making her exhaust herself with explanations.” Baoyu laughed. “Indeed, I was so intent on listening that I forgot I was tiring cousin.” Daiyu laughed. “Talking about these things cheers me up, and it is not at all tiring. I only fear that however much I talk, you will understand none of it.” Baoyu said, “In any case, I shall gradually come to understand it.” As he spoke, he stood up and said, “Truly, cousin, you should rest now. Tomorrow I shall tell Third Cousin and Fourth Cousin and have them both learn, so that they can play for me.” Daiyu laughed. “You certainly know how to enjoy yourself. Even if we all learned to play, since you understand nothing about it, would that not be like playing to—” At that point Daiyu remembered what was weighing on her heart, stopped abruptly, and refused to finish. Baoyu laughed. “As long as you can play, I shall enjoy listening. I do not care whether I am an ox or not.” Daiyu blushed and smiled, while Zijuan and Xueyan both laughed as well. They then went out through the door and saw Qiuwen approaching with a young maid carrying a pot of orchids. She said, “Someone sent four pots of orchids to Her Ladyship. Since they are busy over there and have no leisure to enjoy them, she told us to give one pot to Second Master and one to Miss Lin.” When Daiyu looked, she saw that several stems bore twin blossoms. Her heart suddenly stirred; unable to tell whether she felt joy or sorrow, she stood gazing at them in a daze. Baoyu, however, had his mind fixed entirely on the qin and said, “Now that you have orchids, cousin, you can play ‘The Melody of the Fragrant Orchid.’” On hearing this, Daiyu felt all the more distressed. Back in her room, she looked at the flowers and thought, “When spring comes to plants and trees, their blossoms are fresh and their leaves luxuriant. Yet though I am still young, I am already like willow and reed after three autumns. If my wishes could truly be fulfilled, perhaps I might gradually recover. Otherwise, I fear I shall be like flowers and willows at the close of spring—how could I withstand the urging wind and driving rain?” When her thoughts reached this point, tears once more fell despite herself. Zijuan, watching this from beside her, could not fathom the reason. A moment ago Baoyu had been here and she had been so cheerful; now she was merely looking at the flowers, so why had she suddenly become sorrowful again?

Baoyu said, “In any case, I shall gradually come to understand it.”
As he spoke, he stood up and said, “Truly, cousin, you should rest now.
Tomorrow I shall tell Third Cousin and Fourth Cousin and have them both learn, so that they can play for me.”
Daiyu laughed. “You certainly know how to enjoy yourself.

Even if we all learned to play, since you understand nothing about it, would that not be like playing to—” At that point Daiyu remembered what was weighing on her heart, stopped abruptly, and refused to finish.
Baoyu laughed. “As long as you can play, I shall enjoy listening. I do not care whether I am an ox or not.”
Daiyu blushed and smiled, while Zijuan and Xueyan both laughed as well.

They then went out through the door and saw Qiuwen approaching with a young maid carrying a pot of orchids. She said, “Someone sent four pots of orchids to Her Ladyship. Since they are busy over there and have no leisure to enjoy them, she told us to give one pot to Second Master and one to Miss Lin.”
When Daiyu looked, she saw that several stems bore twin blossoms. Her heart suddenly stirred; unable to tell whether she felt joy or sorrow, she stood gazing at them in a daze.
Baoyu, however, had his mind fixed entirely on the qin and said, “Now that you have orchids, cousin, you can play ‘The Melody of the Fragrant Orchid.’”
On hearing this, Daiyu felt all the more distressed.

Back in her room, she looked at the flowers and thought, “When spring comes to plants and trees, their blossoms are fresh and their leaves luxuriant. Yet though I am still young, I am already like willow and reed after three autumns.

If my wishes could truly be fulfilled, perhaps I might gradually recover. Otherwise, I fear I shall be like flowers and willows at the close of spring—how could I withstand the urging wind and driving rain?”
When her thoughts reached this point, tears once more fell despite herself.
Zijuan, watching this from beside her, could not fathom the reason.
A moment ago Baoyu had been here and she had been so cheerful; now she was merely looking at the flowers, so why had she suddenly become sorrowful again?
